title: The Glassmaker Who Invented Modern Quarantine
event_summary: The Great Council of the Republic of Ragusa, led by rector and physician Jacob of Padua, enacted the 'Trentina' — the world's first institutionalized quarantine law, requiring all ships and travelers arriving from plague-affected areas to isolate on the nearby island of Mrkan or in the town of Cavtat for thirty days before entering the city. This was later extended to forty days (quaranta giorni), giving quarantine its name. The legislation was drafted not by a monarch or military leader but championed by a coalition of merchant-class glassmakers, traders, and civic physicians who understood that Ragusa's survival depended on balancing commerce with disease control.
why_forgotten: Venice's later and more famous lazaretto system (established 1423) has overshadowed Ragusa's earlier innovation, largely because Venetian archives were more widely studied by Western European historians. Ragusa's status as a small Adriatic republic — eventually absorbed into Habsburg and then Yugoslav territories — meant its institutional innovations were treated as footnotes to larger empires' histories. Cold War-era scholarship further marginalized Croatian and Dalmatian contributions to European public health.
why_it_matters: Every modern quarantine protocol, from COVID-19 lockdowns to airport health screenings, descends directly from the legal framework Ragusa pioneered in 1377. The concept that a state has the authority — and obligation — to restrict individual movement to protect collective health was born not in a great empire but in a tiny merchant republic. Ragusa proved that systematic, law-based epidemic response could preserve both lives and economies, a lesson governments are still relearning nearly seven centuries later.
